pages.x: In the tenth century the Bulgarians ruled a great Christian empire across the Balkans, the rival of Byzantium. When the young emperor Basil II came to the throne in Constantinople, a Bulgarian noble, Samuel, led a rising that won back most of the Bulgarian lands, and made his capital at Ohrid.

In 986 Basil marched on Bulgaria himself. On the way home his army was ambushed in a mountain pass called Trajan's Gate and cut to pieces, and Basil barely escaped. It was a humiliation he never forgot.

Basil grew into a grim, tireless soldier. He never married, ate little, wore plain dark clothes, and spent his life on campaign with his men. From 1001 he invaded Bulgaria almost every year, taking its fortresses one by one.

In July 1014 Basil trapped Samuel's army in the pass of Kleidion. The story goes that he had the prisoners blinded, leaving one man in every hundred one eye to lead the rest home. When Samuel saw them, he collapsed, and died two days later. The numbers may be exaggerated, but the story made Basil famous.

Without Samuel, Bulgaria fell apart. In 1018 its last rulers surrendered, and Basil entered Ohrid in triumph, master of the Balkans from the Danube to the Adriatic. Then he went to Athens and gave thanks in the Parthenon, by then a church of the Virgin Mary.

Basil was later called Boulgaroktonos, the Bulgar-slayer. He left Byzantium at the height of its power, with a full treasury. But Bulgaria rose again in 1185, and Bulgarians remember Samuel as a hero.
pts: Forty years of war against Bulgaria
Byzantium at the height of its power
